newsitem.title: NEW ZEALAND: INTERVIEW-Trans Tasman expects re-rating.
newsitem.headline: INTERVIEW-Trans Tasman expects re-rating.

text.p: Trans Tasman Properties Ltd should enjoy an upward re-rating by the market once the planned float of its Australian commercial property assets is under way, Executive Director Chris Canning said on Tuesday.
Canning said in an interview the float of Australian Growth Properties was expected to take place in January.
Trans Tasman has an application before the Sydney City Council for development approval of its George Street site and negotiations are well advanced.
Underwriting details had been held up until approval was granted, he said.
As a result of the listing, Trans Tasman intends to replace A$180 million of Australian debt with new equity. Trans Tasman will retain $A130 million, or 42 percent of the company.

"There will be a really substantial enhancement of the group's balance sheet, which will change quite dramatically again," Canning said. The group's equity to asset ratio would rise to 62 percent from 46.5 percent at present.

"We are anticipating for the (Trans Tasman) group in the region of 35-40 percent earnings per share growth over the next four years and are looking at growth in net asset value over the same period of of 25-30 percent," he said.

Over time, Canning said he expected the Australian arm to dwarf Trans Tasman's New Zealand operations. "The medium term objective is clearly to grow it, with the completion of the George Street development, to A$650 million over the next two years from its current A$300 million."
Tasman Tasman reached its present form through a series of portfolio acquisitions that took place in a mostly depressed market over the last three-and-a-half years.

The evolution started with 46 percent holder SEA Holdings' decision to expand its international investments into Australasia. Brierley Investments Ltd formed an association with SEA involving the Hong Kong-based SEA buying into the BIL property portfolio through an equity exchange.
The entity later became SEABIL Holdings, which listed locally in 1994, concurrently with its purchase of the Fletcher Challenge commercial portfolio.
In 1995, SEABIL chief executive Don Fletcher identified the debt-laden Tasman Properties, formerly Robert Jones Investments, as an investment opportunity.
Fletcher organised a recapitalisation of Tasman, which SEA participated in, enabling SEA and SEABIL to acquire a holding in Tasman at a discount to net asset value.
Last November last year SEABIL and Tasman were amalgamated to form Trans Tasman Properties, with NZ$1.1 billion in assets, about a third of those in Australia.
Canning said the Australian assets were attractive to SEA as it sought an exposure more appropriate to the size of the economy there.
He was not concerned about the proliferation of other property-based investments debuting in Australia as they were mainly trust-based. There was room for both, he added.
The company is about halfway through selling around NZ$150 million in New Zealand assets, mostly in provincial properties, using the proceeds to reduce debt and for renovation.
Trans Tasman closed on Tuesday at NZ$0.74, down one cent, versus a year low of $0.65 and a high of $0.84.
